query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A machine learning regression model that explicitly incorporates defect‐sensitive features—including parameters for defect density and 1 wt.% oxygen contamination—will yield more accurate predictions of electrical conductivity for bulk HfNbTaTiZr than traditional analytical models based on perfect, defect‐free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy in its ideal form and in a realistic form with ~1 wt.% oxygen contamination.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a data‐driven ML regression model trained on a combined dataset of ab initio defect scattering simulations and experimental conductivity measurements.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted over two temperature regimes: a cryogenic range (0–200 K) where quantum and impurity scattering effects are dominant, and a high-temperature range (300–1200 K) where phonon scattering and defect dynamics are significant. Both defect‐free and 1 wt.% oxygen–contaminated samples are considered.
generation.structural_mediator: The effective defect density and oxygen impurity concentration as embedded features within the predictive model.
generation.mechanism: By including features that capture the real scattering mechanisms from lattice defects and oxygen impurities, the ML model can adjust conductivity predictions to reflect the actual microstructural state of the alloy, overcoming the systematic errors of assumptions based solely on perfect crystals.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ML model is expected to produce conductivity predictions that closely track the experimental measurements (with improved statistical accuracy and smaller error margins) across both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes. In contrast, predictions from perfect-crystal analytical models will systematically deviate from observed values, especially in oxygen-contaminated samples.
generation.baseline: Analytical predictions that assume perfect, defect‐free crystal structures.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable within the studied temperature ranges (0–200 K and 300–1200 K) and for samples with up to 1 wt.% oxygen contamination; its performance may be limited if defect densities or impurity levels extend beyond the parameter space of the training data.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement depends on the quality, representativeness, and extent of the defect/impurity information in the training dataset. Uncertainties remain regarding potential additional scattering mechanisms that might not be captured if defect types or oxygen effects differ significantly from those in the training data.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled defect densities and with and without 1 wt.% oxygen contamination. Measure their electrical conductivities across the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes. Compare these measurements against predictions from both the new defect-sensitive ML model and traditional analytical models that assume perfect crystals.
measurements: Electrical conductivity as a function of temperature (0–200 K and 300–1200 K)
Quantification of defect densities (e.g., via TEM or XRD)
Verification of oxygen content (e.g., through spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML model does not show a statistically significant reduction in prediction error compared to the analytical model across both temperature regimes (e.g., if the error reduction is below a pre-defined threshold) or fails to correctly capture the trends introduced by the 1 wt.% oxygen contamination, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Each of these approaches has its own strengths and weaknesses. For example, ab initio and MD are very time-consuming and can hardly be used to predict structures of the alloys in a high-throughput manner. Phenomenological rules are based on empirical observations and are easy for calculations, but the accuracy of their predictions does not exceed 72% []. CALPHAD modeling can be quite throughput, however it requires significant computing resources. In addition, the accuracy of the CALPHAD predictions can be limited due to the absence of a reliable database for HEAs []. The three ML models used in this work are random forest (RF) regressor, gradient boosting regressor (GBR), and XGBoost (XGB) through the Scikit-learn library [], which is also used for data preparation and model assessment. The RF model is an ensemble approach consisting of many decision trees to improve prediction accuracy and reduce overfitting by averaging the trees. The samples of the training dataset may reappear in the single tree due to sampling replacement, also known as bootstrapping. GBR and XGB are multi-purpose machine learning methods that can handle both classification and regression problems. The GBR is a type of ensemble model having an iterative collection of tree models, and it is capable of learning from the previous model’s mistakes. The XGBoost [] is a powerful machine learning method that makes a quick decision by implementing boosted decision trees efficiently and effectively. decision.trend: Early approaches to predicting properties in high‐entropy alloys largely relied on analytical or semi‐empirical models built on the assumption of perfect, defect‐free crystals. For example, analytical models based on the rigid band approximation and phase‐diagram rules were developed to predict phase stability and even electronic properties. However, as shown in PMC6926650, real synthesis methods (e.g., powder metallurgy routes) reveal that processing and minor oxygen contamination can significantly modify the microstructure and, by implication, transport properties. More recently, studies have begun to incorporate machine learning and atomistic simulations – albeit mostly for phase identification or structural prediction – but have not yet tackled conductivity predictions that fully account for defect‐induced scattering and impurity effects over both cryogenic (0–200 K) and high‐temperature (300–1200 K) regimes.
decision.unsolved: The central unsolved challenge is the inability of existing analytical models to capture the real scattering mechanisms arising from defects and trace oxygen impurities. In other words, there is a gap in predictive capability when it comes to describing the temperature‐dependent conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr alloys under realistic conditions.
decision.lever: defect‐sensitive feature inclusion via machine learning regression trained on a combined dataset of ab initio defect scattering simulations and experimental conductivity measurements
decision.why: This approach naturally follows the trend of evolving from idealized analytical predictions to predictive models that incorporate more complex real‐world influences. By explicitly including features sensitive to defect densities and oxygen content – and calibrating them using data from both ab initio simulations (to capture temperature-dependent scattering mechanisms) and experimental measurements – the model can bridge the gap. The hypothesis that such a data‐driven model will predict conductivity accurately over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K (with a defined benchmark on a 1 wt.% oxygen‐contaminated sample) can be directly falsified if the held-out conductivity measurement deviates beyond acceptable error margins, thus making it a testable next step.
